The engine used was a J47-23 turbojet rated at 6060 lbs thrust at 7950 rpm.
Rotating stall was observed to extend axially throughout the instrumented compressor stages and propagate at approximately 50% of rotor speed.
1 to 9 stall zones were measured, with the 7-zone stall being the most predominant.
The extent of the rotating stall range was influenced primarily by the exhaust nozzle setting.
Under normal rated nozzle operation, the maximum vibratory stress was ±26,200 psi in the second-stage blades.
With the closed nozzle to simulate rapid acceleration, the maximum vibratory stress increased to ±60,000 psi in the second stage.
The maximum vibratory stresses in the other stages ranged from ±5,200 to ±17,500 psi.
The high vibratory stresses were due to resonance between the blade frequencies and the fundamental or harmonics of the relative rotating stall frequencies.
Compressor efficiency, pressure ratio, and weight flow were presented for the open, rated, and closed A nozzle settings.
Closed nozzle operation was limited to around 6000 rpm due to approaching limiting turbine temperatures.
Hot-wire anemometers were used to measure the rotating stall, and resistance-wire strain gages were used to measure blade vibration.
The rotating stall occurred from around 50 to 70% of the design compressor speed.
With 1 or 2 stall zones, the pattern would maintain itself until a change in engine speed caused a new pattern.
With 3 to 9 stall zones, the pattern was continually changing, though the 7-zone stall predominated.
The closed nozzle setting accentuated the predominance of the 7-zone stall pattern.
